```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(nnet)
library(purrr)
```

Supplemental equations + semi toy example calculating growth rates and transmission advantages logistic and multinomial variant nowcast models. 


#Supplementary Box 1. Logistic growth

**Sequence observation process**
Adopted from Chen et al., 2021 and Althaus et al., 2021 and Figgins and Bedford., 2025

$$
n_v(t) \sim \text{Binomial}\left(N(t),\ p_v(t)\right)
$$
Where the number of observations of our variant of interest (for example, PANGO lineage B.1.1.7) at time $t$ is $n_v(t)$ and is binomially distributed, $N(t)$ is the number of sequences collected at $t$ and $p_v(t)$ is the expected proportion of sequences at $t$ that are variant $v$ (equivalently, the probability that a given sequence is variant $v$).


**Variant frequency logistic model**
$$
p_v(t) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp{(-\beta_v(t - t_0))}} 
$$
Where $p_v(t)$ is the proportion of sequences that are variant $v$ at time $t$, and $\beta_v$ is the variant's logistic growth rate relative to all other background variants and $t_0$ is the sigmoid midpoint. 

```{r}
Var_freq_logistic_model <- function(beta, t, t0){

  return(1 / (1 + exp(-beta * (t - t0))))
  
}
```


###Example
```{r}
#Read in PANGO sequences from nextstrain
pangonum <- read_tsv("~/growthadvantagecompare/sequences_static/global.tsv") %>% 
  mutate(variant = "pango") %>% 
  rename(name = clade)

pangototn_usa <- pangonum %>% filter(location == "USA") %>% 
  group_by(date) %>% summarise(totn = sum(sequences)) %>% 
  mutate("variant" = "pango")

#Get proportions / day ie p_v(t)
pangoprops_usa <- left_join(pangototn_usa, pangonum %>% filter(location == "USA"), by = "date") %>% 
 mutate(pangoprop = sequences/totn) 

#Plot B.1.1.7
pangoprops_usa %>%
  filter(location == "USA", name == "B.1.1.7", date > as.Date("2020-08-20")) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  filter(date <= date[which.max(pangoprop)]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(date, pangoprop)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = totn), alpha = 0.2, colour = "#2166ac") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion of sequences", size = "Total sequences",
       title = "B.1.1.7 in the USA, rise to peak beginning 2020-08-20") +
  theme_minimal()

#Convert to useable df 
pangoprops_input<- pangoprops_usa %>%
  filter(location == "USA", name == "B.1.1.7", date > as.Date("2020-08-20")) %>% 
   filter(date <= date[which.max(pangoprop)]) %>% #also filter date to only include max proportion date
 mutate(t = as.numeric(date - min(date))) %>% 
  arrange(t) %>% 
  select(date, t, name, totn, pangoprop)

#Write the variant frequency logistic function
#p_v(t) = 1/ (1 + exp(-beta * (t - t0))
#p_v(t) is our input ie pangoprop or the proportion of variant B117 at time t, or p(day)
#we guess that the beta (growth rate) is .05, this is where the function starts searching 
#Alternatively, parameters can be estimated using glm:
# gfit <- glm(pangoprop ~ t,
#             family  = binomial(link = "logit"),
#             weights = totn,
#             data    = pangoprops_input)


#Fit
nfit <- nls(pangoprop ~ 1 / (1 + exp(-beta * (t - t0))),
            data    = pangoprops_input,
            start   = list(beta = 0.05, t0 = max(pangoprops_input$t) / 2), 
            weights = totn)

#Model outputs
coef(nfit)                 
beta  <- coef(nfit)[["beta"]] 

#We get the growth rate to be .036 per day, this is about half what chen and washington et al., get. Our data are fully backfilled, so we know now that B117 did not reach 100% prevalence. As we are fitting to ~75% prevalence, the growth rate we get will be lower.  

t0 <- coef(nfit)[["t0"]]

t_grid<- seq(0, max(pangoprops_input$t, by = 1)) #Making a grid of times using the t from our data

#Lets plug the estimated parameters back into the vaiant frequency logistic model function from Supplementary box 1 and plot the fit 
fit_df <- data.frame(
  t    = t_grid,
  date = min(pangoprops_input$date) + t_grid,
  fit  = Var_freq_logistic_model(beta = beta, t = t_grid, t0 = t0)
)

#Plot the function estimated from our parameters 
ggplot(pangoprops_input, aes(date, pangoprop)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = totn), alpha = 0.4, colour = "#2166ac") +
  geom_line(data = fit_df, aes(date, fit), linewidth = 1, colour = "#b2182b") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = min(pangoprops_input$date) + t0,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion of sequences", size = "Total sequences",
       title = "B.1.1.7 in the USA with logistic fit",
       subtitle = sprintf("beta = %.3f per day; dashed line = 50%% (t0)", beta)) +
  theme_minimal()
```


#Supplementary Box 2. Transmission advantage
Assuming a fixed generation time of $g$, the transmission advantage, or $\Delta_v$ is the $R_t$ of the novel variant over all other variants ie $R_tnovel/R_tbackground$

Chen et al., 2021 uses this parameterization, as do Abousamra et al ., 2024 in the multinomial expansion.

In a multinomial model $R_t, novel\ variant/R_t, reference\ variant$, with the coefficients

$$
\Delta_v = e^{\beta_v* g} = \frac{R_{t,\text{novel}}}{R_{t,\text{background}}} \tag{1b.}
$$
Where $g$ is the generation time, in the same time units as $\beta_v$, assumed equal for both variants and a point estimate in most cases. In the multinomial model, the transmission advantage becomes  $R_t, novel\ variant/R_t, reference\ variant$

```{r}
deltav_fun <- function(beta, g){
  exp(beta*g)
}
```


###Example
```{r}
#Hart, W. S. et al.,2022 gt of 5.5

g <- 5.5 #Generation time

delta_b117 <- deltav_fun(beta = beta, g = g)

delta_b117

#The Rt of B.1.1.7 is 1.22 times higher than circulating background variants 
```

#Supplementary Box 3. Multinomial growth
Adapted from Abousamra et al ., 2024

**Sequence observation process**

$$
\left(n_1(t), \dots, n_K(t)\right) \sim \text{Multinomial}\left(N(t);\ p_1(t), \dots, p_K(t)\right)
$$
here $n_1(t)$ through $n_K(t)$ are the numbers of sequences of variant 1 to variant $K$ at time $t$, $N(t)$ is the number of sequences collected at $t$, and $p_1(t)$ through $p_K(t)$ are the expected proportions of sequences at $t$ that are variant 1 to variant $K$ (equivalently, the probability that a given sequence is each variant). The variant of interest $v$ is one of these $K$ variants.

**Variant frequency multinomial model**

$$
p_v(t) = \frac{\exp(f_{0,v} + \beta_v t)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(f_{0,k} + \beta_k t)}
$$
Where $p_v(t)$ is the expected proportion of sequences that are variant $v$ at time $t$, and $\beta_v$ is the logistic growth rate of variant $v$ relative to the reference variant, $f_{0,v}$ and $f_{0,k}$ are the log initial frequencies of variants $v$ and $k$, respectively, relative to a reference variant, which has $\beta$ and $f_0$ set to zero. 

```{r}
Var_freq_multinomial_model <- function(f0, beta, t){
  
  return(exp(f0 + beta*t)/sum(exp(f0 + beta*t))) #for every f0 and beta, multiply by t 
  
}
```

###Example 
```{r}
#Lets find the most prevalent variants using the same time window as before
#Set number of variants to model / group
K_variants <- 3

top_K <- pangoprops_usa %>%
  filter(location == "USA",
         date > as.Date("2020-08-20") & date < as.Date("2020-12-20")) %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  summarise(total_seq = sum(sequences)) %>%
  slice_max(total_seq, n = K_variants) %>%
  pull(name)

#Peak date for B117
peak_date <- pangoprops_usa %>%
  filter(location == "USA", name == "B.1.1.7",
         date > as.Date("2020-08-20"), totn >= 50) %>%
  slice_max(pangoprop, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  pull(date)



lineages_to_show <- unique(c(top_K, "B.1.1.7"))
lineages_to_show   


#Group all variants as other if not present in top K
#This is the "grouping" that makes comparisons between model outputs challenging
#"Other" is grouped in a subjective way.

pangoprops2_input <- pangoprops_usa %>%
  filter(location == "USA", date > as.Date("2020-08-20"), date <= peak_date) %>%
  mutate(name = if_else(name %in% lineages_to_show, name, "Other")) %>%
  group_by(date, name) %>%
  summarise(sequences = sum(sequences), totn = first(totn), .groups = "drop") %>%
  complete(nesting(date, totn), name, fill = list(sequences = 0)) %>%
  mutate(t = as.numeric(date - min(date)),
         pangoprop = sequences / totn) %>%
  arrange(t, name) 


pangoprops2_input %>%
  ggplot(aes(date, pangoprop, colour = name)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = totn), alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion of sequences", size = "Total sequences",
       colour = "Lineage",
       title = "SARS-CoV-2 lineages in the USA, 2020-08-20 to B.1.1.7 peak") +
  theme_minimal()


#Use nnet to estimate the parameters
#Choose B.1 as our reference variable using factor
multinom_fit <- multinom(name ~ t, data = (pangoprops2_input %>%
  mutate(name = relevel(factor(name), ref = "B.1"))),                       weights = sequences, 
 maxit = 1000) 

#Extract the parameters 
params <- data.frame(
  lineage = c("B.1", rownames(coef(multinom_fit))),
  f0_multi      = c(0, coef(multinom_fit)[, "(Intercept)"]),
  beta_multi    = c(0, coef(multinom_fit)[, "t"])
)


#Time grid
t_grid <- seq(0, max(pangoprops2_input$t, by = 1))


#Map over every value of t using the parameters nnet estimated using the multinomial function from Supplementary Box 3
multinom_out <- purrr::map(t_grid, ~ tibble(
    t       = .,
    lineage = params$lineage,
    fitted  = Var_freq_multinomial_model(f0 = params$f0_multi,
                                  beta = params$beta_multi,
                                  t = .)
  )) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind()


multinom_out <- multinom_out %>%
  rename(name = lineage) %>%
  mutate(date = min(pangoprops2_input$date) + t)

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = pangoprops2_input,
             aes(date, pangoprop, colour = name, size = totn), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = multinom_out,
            aes(date, fitted, colour = name), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion of sequences", colour = "Lineage",
       size = "Total sequences",
       title = "SARS-CoV-2 lineages in the USA with multinomial fit") +
  theme_minimal()

#Lets find the growth advantage of B.1.1.7 vs B.1 

g <- 5.5 #Generation time 

delta_muti <- data.frame(delta_v = deltav_fun(params$beta_multi, g),
           variant = params$lineage)


delta_muti

#The Rt of B.1.1.7 is 1.42 higher than B.1 in the multinomial model
```
